data.title: CSL Seqirus blasted for ‘multiple and prolonged deficiencies’
data.description:
A U.K. drug marketing watchdog has slammed CSL Seqirus for “multiple and prolonged deficiencies” in its systems, governance and oversight.

The PMCPA, a self-regulatory body in the U.K., began investigating CSL Seqirus after the flu vaccine manufacturer voluntarily admitted problems with the disclosure of payments. CSL Seqirus failed to disclose two grants to a French healthcare organization. The company named an intermediary, rather than the ultimate recipient, as the beneficiary of a third payment.  

“Payments totalling an excess of 700,000 pounds ($925,000) had been made to a healthcare organization without the required documentation or public disclosure,” the PMCPA said in its report. “CSL Seqirus had only become aware of the issue following a grant application from the same healthcare organization in 2025.”

The company rejected the 2025 grant application, leading it to investigate earlier payments. After finding fault with its disclosures of the earlier payments, which it made from 2020 to 2022, CSL Seqirus voluntarily told the PMCPA that it had breached the U.K. marketing code.

Investigating the case, the PMCPA found that CSL Seqirus failed to identify the absence of valid written agreements with the healthcare organization for three years. The PMCPA voiced concerns about “the number of governance and oversight processes that had failed, including the company's arrangements for approving grants, maintaining accurate records and ensuring the disclosure of transfers of value.”

The cumulative nature of the failings led the PMCPA to conclude CSL Seqirus had suffered wider systemic issues, not an isolated occurrence. CSL Seqirus admitted to a lack of oversight and governance from 2020 to 2022 but expressed confidence in the practices it established in 2024, noting that they led it to reject the 2025 grant application. Efforts to further improve oversight are underway. 

“We are undertaking a review of our current processes to assess whether further enhancements are needed to prevent any future deviations and ensure continued compliance with both internal standards and external regulatory requirements,” the company told the PMCPA.

CSL Seqirus’ admission failed to spare the company from the PMCPA’s harshest censure. The watchdog ruled that the company brought discredit upon, or reduced confidence in, the pharmaceutical industry by failing to properly disclose the grants.

data.title: Free lunches for clinicians bloat prescription bills: review
data.description:
Promotional interactions between clinicians and pharmaceutical companies are probably associated with harmful outcomes, according to a Cochrane review that assessed free meals, ads and other dealings.

The researchers wanted to understand the impact of the interactions on the appropriateness, quantity and cost of prescriptions, as well as on formulary requests. To answer their questions, the team looked at 93 studies, most of which were run in the U.S. Two-thirds of the studies assessed the effect of payments, gifts or other transfers of value, while other papers analyzed the impact of ads and educational activities.

Armed with data on millions of doctors, the researchers reached the firmest conclusions on the effect of gifts and payments. Such financial transactions increase inappropriate prescribing and the quantity of prescriptions and probably raise prescription costs, the researchers said. 

Digging deeper, the researchers linked the number of meals doctors receive to their prescribing of the promoted product across seven drug classes. Lead author Barbara Mintzes, Ph.D., a pharmaceutical policy specialist at the University of Sydney, Australia, outlined the importance of the finding.  

“Doctors often think that this is trivial and doesn’t influence them, that they ‘can’t be bought for the price of a sandwich,’ but the data shows this is an effective marketing strategy,” Mintzes said in a statement. “The more free meals a doctor receives, the more likely they are to prescribe less appropriate or more expensive drugs.”

The datasets on pharma company advertising or education aimed at doctors are smaller, covering fewer than 1,000 to more than 150,000 physicians, depending on the question. The researchers concluded that ads and educational activities probably increase the quantity of prescriptions. The activities may increase inappropriate prescribing and the costs of prescriptions, the researchers said. 

After reviewing seven studies, the researchers were uncertain whether free samples affect physicians. An analysis of eight papers on conflict-of-interest policies yielded firmer conclusions. Policies restricting or managing interactions between drugmakers and doctors probably boost prescribing appropriateness and may decrease prescribing quantity, the researchers said. The effect on costs is uncertain.

data.title: Melissa explains it all in menopause team up with Bayer
data.description:
Bayer is teaming up with American actress and director Melissa Joan Hart to boost awareness about hot flashes treatment Lynkuet by tapping her personal experiences.

Up to 80% of women report having hot flashes at some point during the menopausal transition, and the symptom is one of the main factors that prompts women to seek menopause treatment, according to Bayer. 

Meanwhile, more than one-third of women report experiencing severe vasomotor symptoms, which can last a decade or more after the last menstrual period, the company has said.

And it is a growing issue as by 2030, Bayer estimates that the global population of women experiencing menopause will increase to 1.2 billion, with some 47 million women entering this stage in their life each year.

To help boost awareness of these symptoms, and Bayer’s hot flashes drug Lynkuet, Hart will share her personal experience with moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause “to help women recognize their symptoms and to encourage more proactive treatment conversations with their healthcare providers,” according to a statement. Hart is not however currently using the drug. 

“I thought my days of waking up in the middle of the night were behind me after raising my kids,” said in Hart in a release. “Then menopause came along. I knew hot flashes could happen, but I didn't expect them to affect me the way they did. I found myself sometimes waking up at night, this time not because of my kids, but because of severe hot flashes.

“I know I’m not the only woman who has experienced moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause. I hope sharing my experience encourages women to talk openly with their healthcare providers about their symptoms and treatment options, like Lynkuet.”

She is also asking women to learn more about their treatment options via several initiatives, including a Reddit Ask Me Anything campaign.

Related

Bayer taps Gabrielle Union-Wade as face of menopause med Lynkuet

The Big Pharma first recruited Gabrielle Union-Wade back in January to serve as a celebrity endorser for the then newly launched medication.

Union-Wade has long been a vocal advocate for a wide range of causes, including many affecting women’s health—from reproductive justice to breast cancer awareness—and is a Lynkuet user herself. 

It’s been almost a year now since the FDA approved Bayer’s dual neurokinin (NK) targeted therapy to treat moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms—comprising hot flashes and night sweats—in people with menopause.

Bayer projects annual peak sales for Lynkuet to reach around 1 billion euros ($1.2 billion) globally at peak. 

Lynkuet comes in a soft gel capsule and is taken once a day at bedtime. The drug competes with Astellas’ Veozah, another nonhormonal menopause symptom drug that targets NK3 but not NK1 and has been on the market since 2023. 

Women with menopause also have access to a third nonhormonal treatment in the U.S. in Brisdelle, a reformulation of the decades-old antidepressant paroxetine that was cleared to control hot flashes back in 2013.

Aside from those options, hormone therapy incorporating estrogen alone or with progesterone has long been a benchmark treatment for vasomotor symptoms. Nevertheless, hormone-based therapies aren’t necessarily a good fit for all women, and they carry known risks such as endometrial and breast cancers.

data.title: Sanofi drafts NBA champ to spread COVID, Nuvaxovid awareness
data.description:
2026 NBA Champion Karl-Anthony Towns knows both ball and COVID-19. As Sanofi’s newest celeb spokesperson for non-mRNA COVID vaccine Nuvaxovid, the athlete is sharing his personal experience with COVID and encouraging others to talk vaccination with their healthcare providers. 

The campaign will see Towns helping to drive COVID awareness and education through a series of digital and social media activations, Sanofi said in a press release, building on the six-time NBA All-Star’s understanding of the importance of “preparation, performance and staying healthy.”

“With respiratory virus season fast approaching and preparing for the upcoming basketball season, being proactive about protecting my health remains a priority for me,” Towns commented in the release. “That's why I'm partnering with Sanofi to encourage people, especially those at increased risk, to talk with their healthcare provider to learn about their COVID-19 vaccination options, including Nuvaxovid." 

As Towns explained, COVID-19 impacted his family “in a profound way,” with those experiences shaping his stance on health and “the importance of taking steps to help protect myself,” he said.

Related

Sanofi hits the pickleball court in education push for COVID vax Nuvaxovid

“Karl-Anthony brings an authentic and deeply personal perspective to raising awareness about COVID-19 vaccination,” explained Sanofi’s head of vaccines for North America, Kimberly Tutwiler, in a statement. “At a time when many eligible people remain unvaccinated, helping people better understand their available vaccination options remains an important public health priority.” 

The company is “proud to partner” with Towns to encourage “informed conversations” about vaccine options, Tutwiler added. 

It’s been a historic year for Sanofi’s new paid spokesperson, who helped lead the New York Knicks to their first NBA championship win in over 50 years. In an interview shared by Sanofi, the star center and forward opened up about losing his mother and several other close family members to COVID. 

“I know firsthand how devastating this virus can be, and I want the people to understand that this virus can still have serious consequences and that protecting your health is something worth taking seriously,” Towns said. 

As COVID season picks up this fall, Sanofi has taken to more than one athletic court to promote Nuvaxovid. Last month, the French pharma partnered with USA Pickleball for a joint “Serve Up Protection” campaign targeting older adults through multimedia education, fan experiences, “trusted pickleball voices,” and a presence at major events, such as USA Pickleball’s National Championships this November in San Diego. 

Protein-based Nuvaxovid presents an alterative option to the mRNA shots made by Moderna and Pfizer. Originally developed by Novavax and handed over to Sanofi through a co-collaboration licensing agreement that went through last year, the vaccine earned full FDA approval last May in adults aged 65 years and older and people between the ages of 12 and 64 who have at least one underlying health condition. 

Sanofi emphasizes that having multiple vaccine options is key for sustainable public health strategies and may help healthcare systems to address vaccine hesitancy. 

In the U.S., 17.5% of adults 18 years old and older reported getting a COVID vaccine for the 2025-2026 season as of Feb. 22, according to the CDC, while IQVIA tracked an estimated 20.82 million doses given in retail pharmacies and 2.47 million administered in medical offices as of April.

data.title: The Future of Healthcare Marketing Isn’t More Media. It’s Better Intelligence.
data.description:
Author: Andrew Burkus, Head of Thought Leadership at IQVIA Digital.

Healthcare marketers have never had more ways to reach an audience.

Programmatic advertising. Connected TV. Social media. Digital point of care. Email. Endemic media. AI-enabled decision engines that automate processes across existing channels.

Yet despite this expansion, many organizations are confronting a surprising reality: more channels have not necessarily created more clarity.   Organizations are not suffering from a lack of information. They are struggling to distinguish meaningful signal from growing volumes of activity, content and data. The challenge is no longer simply reaching people. It is understanding who matters, recognizing meaningful signals and acting with confidence as those signals emerge across an increasingly fragmented ecosystem.

The industry is entering a Signal Economy, where competitive advantage comes not from access to more media or information, but from the ability to recognize meaningful change, transform information into intelligence and act before the opportunity passes.

The End of the Channel-First Era

For years, healthcare marketing strategies have largely been organized around channels. Teams built plans around social, search, programmatic, email or endemic placements, and success was often measured within each environment.

But healthcare decision-making doesn’t happen in channels.

Healthcare professionals and patients move fluidly among research sources, AI-generated answers, peer networks, medical publications, educational content, brand resources and clinical evidence. Each interaction creates an observable signal, but isolated activity rarely tells the complete story.

At the same time, healthcare journeys have become more complex and less predictable. Patients face barriers to diagnosis, treatment initiation, access and adherence, while healthcare professionals navigate growing volumes of information and competing demands. Signals help organizations identify emerging needs, moments of friction and opportunities to intervene before traditional performance metrics fully reveal them.

The most effective marketers are increasingly asking different questions:

  • Which audiences matter most?
  • What signals indicate interest, intent, unmet need or friction?
  • How does engagement evolve over time?
  • What outcomes are we trying to create?
  • How can today’s learning improve tomorrow’s decision?

These questions shift the focus from media execution to audience intelligence.

Identity Becomes the Foundation

The more fragmented the ecosystem becomes, the more difficult it is to maintain a consistent understanding of who is being reached.

Every handoff between systems can introduce gaps in visibility. Audience definitions change. Reporting methodologies differ. Measurements become difficult to reconcile.

Identity provides the connective tissue that transforms isolated observations into coherent understanding. It helps determine whether fragmented signals reflect the same healthcare professional, patient, journey or underlying story.

Without that foundation, organizations risk optimizing against noise while believing they are responding to signal.

Intelligence as the New Operating Model

The goal is not to centralize every platform or force all activity into a single destination. It is to create an operating model where signals generated across planning, activation, measurement and engagement continuously inform the next decision, regardless of channel.

In this model, audience intelligence doesn’t stop once a campaign launches. Measurement isn’t an end-of-quarter reporting exercise. Insights generated today become inputs for tomorrow’s decisions. The organization learns continuously rather than campaign by campaign.

The next step is to move toward always-on, embedded decision intelligence.

  AI can accelerate analysis, surface patterns and automate workflows. But AI does not create signal. It amplifies the quality, context and identity resolution of the information guiding it. Its value ultimately depends on the strength of the signals it receives.

Why Outcomes Matter More Than Impressions

Healthcare marketers have always faced a unique responsibility. Success isn’t simply about generating awareness or engagement. It is ultimately about influencing meaningful healthcare decisions.

Impressions, clicks and engagement rates remain useful digital indicators, but they represent only part of the story in healthcare.

A signal is more than a datapoint. It is an indication that something meaningful may be changing before traditional performance measures fully reveal it. The better question is not simply whether a signal works, but when, where and for whom it matters most.

Healthcare measurement must connect digital signals to what is actually happening in the real world. Linking campaign activity with real-world healthcare data, including claims tied to HCPs and patient activity, can help marketers understand whether they are reaching the right audiences at the right time, identify meaningful shifts and determine the next-best actions for campaign optimization. That means looking beyond clicks and impressions to measures such as: 

  • Audience quality compared to healthcare targets
  • Incremental reach
  • HCP and patient engagement
  • Barriers across the care journey
  • Channel contribution
  • Business and healthcare outcomes for net impact

Measurement should not simply explain what happened. It should help determine what happens next. The future of measurement is not retrospective validation. It is decision intelligence embedded into planning, optimization and action.

A More Intelligent Future

The next phase of healthcare marketing will be defined by intelligence rather than scale.

Audience strategies will become more dynamic. Measurement will become more connected. AI-enabled decision engines will help teams identify opportunities earlier and adapt faster.

But technology alone is not the story. The bigger shift is strategic.

Healthcare marketing is moving from channel-first thinking to audience-first thinking. From isolated metrics to measurable outcomes. From managing campaigns to building systems that learn continuously.

More media is not the advantage. Better intelligence is.

The organizations that can connect disparate, often fragmented pieces of information into a deeper understanding of the people they serve will create the most value.

In the Signal Economy, more information is not the advantage. The advantage belongs to organizations that can recognize meaningful signal, transform it into intelligence, and act before the moment passes.

data.title: National Fragility Index spotlights drug supply-chain problems
data.description:
The National Fragility Index, launched by the API Innovation Center, warns that more than 550 million prescriptions filled in the U.S. in 2023 were for drugs ranked as having high or severe vulnerability to potential supply chain disruptions. 

The index, which debuted Tuesday and is produced by APIIC in conjunction with industry supported market intelligence and supply chain platform QYOBO, was designed to provide detailed tracking of pharmaceutical supply chain risks in the United States. 

The inaugural NFI study focused on more than 400 drugs, covering 131 treatment categories. Fourteen were rated severe and 71 as high fragility, which combined represents one in five medicines facing supply-chain stress, the group said in a press release.

Almost 6 in 10 of the drugs analyzed by the NFI have experienced at least one shortage, with the average length of those shortages lasting more than two years, APIIC added.

Two drugs highlighted in the report were pantoprazole, a widely used stomach-acid medicine with 34 million prescriptions filled in 2024, and metoprolol, the most prescribed systemic beta-blocker in the U.S., with more than 58 million prescriptions filled in 2024.

Pantoprazole was rated severe on the index, which found that just Just 5.6% of the drug dispensed domestically comes from a U.S.-based finished-dose manufacturer. It has reported shortages five times since 2015.

Related

Sinking prices for generic meds a major factor in US shortage crisis: report

Metoprolol, which was rated high, had 58 million scripts filled in 2024. The index found there is no domestic source for APIs used to produce the drug, which has experienced two shortages since 2015, with each shortage lasting an average of nearly five years.

According to the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, at least 11 of the 86 essential medicines have a U.S. manufacturer, however, none are currently supplying U.S. drugmakers.

“We cannot know whether our investments are strengthening the drug supply unless we can measure the risks they are meant to address,” said Natalie de Graaf, VP and general manager for data analytics, AI and machine learning solutions at St. Louis-based APIIC, in a statement. “The National Fragility Index gives decision-makers a starting point. It helps them see which supply chains need attention today and track whether their choices are making a difference.”

The index comes in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic that exposed problems in the global pharma supply chain, with pushes by both the Biden and Trump administrations to “on-shore” more drug manufacturing in the U.S. Its focus is to spot problems in order to pivot supply chains for national security and bolster U.S. drug manufacturing capabilities, APIIC said.

“For years, pharmaceutical companies have used our supply chain intelligence to make decisions with confidence,” Markus Felgenhauer, co-founder and CEO of QYOBO, said in a statement. “We’re excited to bring that same intelligence to the public sector, giving policymakers a clear view of supply dependencies and manufacturing sites around the globe, so they can direct resources where they will strengthen the resilience of the U.S. drug supply and ultimately benefit American patients.”

data.title: Rising Stars: VML Health's Molly Kanofsky
data.description:
Molly Kanofsky had it all planned out. After years of picking up medical experience and focusing on the clinical side of the healthcare industry, she was going to go to back to school to become a physician assistant (PA) after graduating from the University of Delaware with her Bachelor of Applied Science. But instead of what was once her chosen path as a physician assistant, Kanofsky now finds herself in the pharma marketing world with VML Health after an unexpected career detour.

The door that closed on PA school opened to a new best-of-both-worlds career that merges her passion for healthcare and her creative abilities. After almost two years with BGB Group and another two with Havas Health Network in New York, Kanofsky started with VML Health in August as an account supervisor. 

In a Q&A for Fierce Pharma Marketing’s “Rising Stars” series, Kanofsky explains her early career pivot, the excitement of learning as you go on a new project and the importance of leading with empathy and compassion. 

Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

FPMK: What inspired you to pursue a career in pharma marketing, and what keeps you motivated in your current role?

I took a very unconventional route into pharma marketing. Even in high school, in college, I spent so much of my time pursuing the career of a PA, physician assistant. So I was volunteering in hospitals. I was working as a medical assistant, gaining as much clinical experience as I can, and then, unfortunately, I applied to PA school and I didn't get in. I was absolutely devastated. I feel like I was so tunnel visioned on that one goal that it was just really upsetting for me. I felt like I had failed, and I had no idea what I was supposed to do next because I really hadn't thought of any other career paths for me. 

But I kind of realized that I wanted to go into healthcare because of impacting people's lives and just doing something that helps other people, so I just really needed to figure out another way to do it, and quite quickly because I'd graduated college and obviously needed an income of sorts. So my cousin actually worked for BGB Group for years, and he loved it. I heard about pharma marketing through him, and then I kind of researched what that would look like. And once I got in it, I realized I was able to combine my love for healthcare and then also my creative side, and it honestly just all clicked. And I realized, wow, this is a great field for me. 

What keeps me motivated? I feel like there's two big things for me. More than anything is the people I work with. I've been really lucky to work on teams where everyone brings something different to the table, and I've learned so much from the people around me, so that is incredible. And then, second, I also love seeing something go from an idea on a page or just a simple conversation with your client or your team, and then that's actually put out into the real world. There's something very incredibly rewarding about being involved from the very beginning, working through all the challenges along the way with your team, and then finally seeing the end result make an impact on so many lives.

FPMK: What has been the most rewarding or challenging project that you've worked on so far?

So for the first couple years of my career, I was really in more of the traditional HCP marketing side of things. Then I had the opportunity in my last job to work on an account that was focused on partnering with physician influencers in the narcolepsy space to create content on a variety of social platforms, which is truly something I never heard of, like never heard before. It was still HCP to HCP education, but through a channel and format that was completely new to me and pretty new to my client as well. So because it was new for my client, we were really building a lot of the processes as we went, we worked in lockstep, figuring out what that should look like, what worked and what didn't, and how to bring the ideas to life within all the parameters we needed to work within. 

I found myself getting more hands-on experience than I ever expected. There were moments where we needed a social mock-up to help visualize an idea, and I'd find myself in Canva putting together something. It was really everyone learning and figuring things out as we went. So there was very much a mentality of whatever needs to get done, we will figure out a way to do so, even if it wasn't like a typical process or like your standard timeline to get things done. We were like, 'we're gonna do whatever it takes to get this done, and we will figure it out.' So it was definitely one of the most challenging projects I've worked on because there were so many firsts, but that's also why it made it so rewarding as well. 
Molly Kanofsky FPMK rising star

FPMK: What advice would you give to people who worked in pharma marketing for decades?

I think the best thing someone with decades of experience can do is continue to share that experience generously while staying open to the people around them. I've been incredibly lucky to work with people who are much smarter and more experienced than I am, and I love that being around them makes me better. 

I learn so much from how they think, how they approach challenges, and the perspective that they bring, but I also think the strongest teams recognize that everyone has something to contribute, regardless of how long they've been in the industry. And to me, that comes back to leading with empathy and compassion. When people feel supported, respected, and comfortable bringing their perspectives to the table, everyone learns from each other, and ultimately the work is better for it.

FPMK: What do you like to do when you're not working?

I live in New York, so my most favorite thing to do is really just walking everywhere, exploring different neighborhoods, and trying new restaurants. There's so many things, so many restaurants opening all the time. So it's so fun just going somewhere and trying something new. I spend as much time as possible with my boyfriend, my friends, my family, and I love traveling. I'm pretty much always planning my next trip. I'm actually going to Italy at the end of this week, so I'm so excited!

data.title: How drugmakers can capitalize on the GLP-1 'consumer overlay'
data.description:
With the advent of powerful GLP-1 medications from Novo and Eli Lilly, the conversation is shifting around obesity’s status as a chronic disease, as is the understanding of how tackling weight can trigger a multitude of downstream health benefits.

At the same time, however, a confluence of factors, from social media buzz to the proliferation of a compounding pharmacy cottage industry, has fundamentally changed the way many patients seek access to drugs like Novo’s Wegovy and Lilly’s Zepbound.

More aware and information-armed than ever, patients’ appetite for GLP-1s means drugmakers looking to ride the current and next-gen weight loss waves must fundamentally rethink their marketing playbooks and adapt to a changing commercial landscape that may soon extend well beyond hormone receptor agonists.

That’s the read of the room according to Kristin Ciriello Pothier, U.S. and Americas region life sciences sector leader and global deal advisory and strategy leader for healthcare and life sciences at “Big Four” accounting firm KPMG.

As the commercial landscape for obesity treatments has evolved, it now “truly meshes consumer health with real-life therapeutics,” she said in a recent interview.

The successes of the GLP-1 class for chronic weight management “introduced consumer overlay over a historically physician-driven therapeutic area,” Pothier explained, noting that despite the potency of the drugs, popular interest meant the GLP-1s “almost were taken out of physicians’ hands” and placed into those of the consumer.

The magnitude of consumer sway in the market is unprecedented in the pharmaceutical realm, Pothier said, noting that one obvious driving factor is the ubiquity of social media in today’s world.

Meanwhile, the swift rise of consumer-driven platforms offering treatments for sexual health, hair loss and other conditions through companies like Hims & Hers and Ro, along with direct-to-consumer diagnostics that emerged even earlier, has made the virtual pharmacy an increasingly popular avenue for patients to access their medications in recent years.

What that means for the branded industry, in Pothier’s estimation, is that this “has totally changed the way that pharmaceutical companies are thinking about their commercial launches and their branding overall.”

One point to consider is that patients are also coming into treatment conversations with a stronger understanding of what they want and expect from a medicine, Pothier explained.

Providers, too, need to be more knowledgeable about dosing and how GLP-1s are being used in actual practice, she added, flagging trends like microdosing. This also requires knowledge-sharing by drugmakers so that providers aren’t “pushed out of the loop” in turn, Pothier said.

Ultimately, figuring out how to get healthcare providers back into GLP-1 conversations will be critical to the success of next-generation launches, she figures, given that the current reality means patients can seek compounded versions of GLP-1 drugs through online platforms and other outlets, sometimes after completing an online questionnaire.

That is “very concerning” to the pharma companies themselves, no doubt, and they should in turn make a push to ensure that marketing and maintenance campaigns remain a focus of commercial launches to retain market share, she added. Whereas traditional launches might have been able to scale back marketing pushes after some time, that's likely not a luxury branded GLP-1 players can afford in the current commercial environment.

When it comes to the drug class and maintaining both market share and public attention, “it’s still a competitive race even a couple of years in,” Pothier said.

Another catalyst is patients’ growing understanding that GLP-1s can do more than help them lose weight, with benefits that extend to other measures of cardiometabolic health.

“The consumer-driven parts of that have awakened more and more patients to take care of their health,” Pothier said. “However, at the same time, that means that the pharmaceutical companies really have to be thoughtful about their approach.”

“It’s not just the commercials at halftime at the Super Bowl,” Pothier said of the evolving landscape, noting that there is now a “constant awakening and back and forth with the consumer and the provider.”

That holistic view of health, along with a desire to meet consumers where they are, helped shape the rebrand that Wegovy and Ozempic maker Novo announced last month, adopting the new mantra that "lasting health starts now."

Reflecting on the change, Novo CEO Mike Doustdar told Fierce that the tagline “also opens up the room for us to explore more,” and in particular “where the future will take us scientifically.” He also noted that the move comes out of a desire to respond to how patients see themselves, which is often more nuanced than seeing themselves simply as a consumer or a person managing a chronic disease.

“[I]nstead of getting into a judgment call of what to call our customers or those we serve—patients or consumers—let’s talk about health,” Doustdar said.

As for capturing the holistic appetite of GLP-1 patients, drugmakers ought to be partnering with other companies to provide a “total solution” for patients, according to KPMG's Pothier, who pointed to additional treatments like supplements for nausea and hair loss medications that are ramping up in popularity alongside incretins, not to mention resultant shifts in consumer behavior related to areas like food, snacking and even clothing purchases.

The ability to tailor care on a personal level will likely be one of the biggest strengths of the next slate of commercial GLP-1 winners. Differences in titration that account for unique patient needs could be a major boon for GLP-1 makers, and delivery methods and supply chain preparedness will be crucial too, Pothier said.

Novo has apparently heard that call.

At the company's Capital Markets Day in September, Doustdar admitted that "'consumers' ... was not in our vocabulary last time we met," but with the boom in interest in the GLP-1 market, Novo is now unveiling plans for what it calls a "Consumer Rx" segment.

"This is where serious condition prescription medication meets incredibly strong consumer demand,” he said during the Novo event.

Earlier this year, Doustdar had also hinted in an interview with Bloomberg that Novo would be open to exploring increasingly interrelated, appearance-facing therapeutic areas like skincare and hair loss.

Metabolic medicine archrival Eli Lilly may be adopting a similar tack, too, with Endpoints News last week flagging a new job posting from the Indianapolis Big Pharma that highlighted aesthetic health as an emerging and strategically significant area for the company.

Surging interest in fields such as hair loss has also given a recent lift to companies like Veradermics, which is working on an oral reformulation of the molecule behind Rogaine and whose CEO expects similar consumer-tinged trends to play out, buoyed by the recent precedent set by GLP-1s.

data.title: Noom puts a spooky voice to the threat of weight regain
data.description:
The bright, sunny shots of Noom’s chief wellness ambassador Rebel Wilson seen in the debut of the digital health company’s “Lose for Keeps” campaign are nowhere to be found in its latest spot, which puts a spooky new voice to the fears many GLP-1 users have. 

Noom’s “Lose for Keeps” campaign launched this summer as one of its “largest brand investments to date,” Noom said at the time. Two national TV, streaming, social and digital ads featuring Wilson showcased Noom’s in-app resources for building healthy habits that can help the weight lost on GLP-1 medicines stay off.  

The same premise takes a darker, comedic tone in its newest “Noom PSA – Weight Regain Doesn’t Care.” In the 30-second spot, a young woman records herself in her dimly lit apartment, explaining how she’s lost 20 pounds after three months on a GLP-1. To this, her TV turns on to say in a snarky-robot voice, “weight regain doesn’t care.”

A subtle horror movie sound effect keeps the vibe creepy as the scene switches to the women in her kitchen, this time excitedly telling her phone camera that her labs are improving. 

“That’s nice. Weight regain doesn’t care,” her smart speaker interrupts. 

The startled woman drops her phone as her Roomba vacuum joins in on the spooky fun, taunting, “weight regain will find you!” 

Even her smoke detector has something to say, flashing red and alerting its owner that “studies show you’ll regain the weight in 18 months.” 

Related

Actress Rebel Wilson pairs GLP-1s and healthy habits to lose weight 'for keeps' in new Noom campaign

This causes the panicked GLP-1 user to scream as the creepy background noise swells. Upon frantically grabbing her phone, the horror movie atmosphere lifts as the woman quickly finds relief in the Noom app, which shows her a screen of “GLP-1s + healthy habits.” 

Now, with nothing to fear, she talks back to her electric kettle, which repeats the “weight regain does not care” mantra. “But Noom does,” the woman replies, triumphantly unplugging the device. 

“Noom members keep off 2x more weight after stopping a GLP-1,” a voiceover and on-screen text read as the woman walks away at the end of the ad. 

“When weight regain feels like the villain in your story… Noom helps you fight back,” the company wrote in the description of the video. “With the tools and support to build lasting habits, you can take charge of what happens next.”

Noom, which bills itself as the “leading behavior change company,” has spent 15 years studying what “actually makes weight loss last,” it said in a press release earlier this summer. The free Noom app leans on psychology, coaching, AI technology and grounded research to help users maintain their health and weight loss goals. 

To further highlight its weight-loss prowess, Noom is adding more patient voices to the mix with a new series of testimonials. The short videos highlight Noom users Janet and Joe, who share their experience using Noom as a “very long-term solution,” as Janet said in her testimonial.

Noom offers specific GLP-1 and low-dose or “micro-dose” GLP-1 programs that pairs the medicine with personalized support and tailored treatment plans. The company has been in the GLP-1 game even before the obesity market blew up with the introduction of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy and Eli Lilly’s Zepbound, with Noom partnering with Novo back in 2019 to support patients using its older Saxenda.

data.title: Gilead rolls out disease-specific wellness tools with Calm app
data.description:
Gilead Sciences is taking a step into the wellness space to support patients with chronic diseases by offering resources that go beyond physical health. The company is partnering with mindfulness app Calm to provide curated content for those impacted by cancer, HIV and liver conditions. 

More than one-third of people living with HIV in the U.S. experience depression, while 28% have an anxiety disorder, according to Gilead and Calm. Additionally, those with HIV often struggle with stigma that can stir up feelings of shame and anxiety. 

Meanwhile, about 50% of people with cancer experience distress, with some two in ten people with cancer reporting symptoms of depression. For those with liver conditions such as primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), symptoms such as fatigue, chronic itch and brain fog can take a toll on daily life, Gilead points out.  

Ahead of World Mental Health Day on Oct. 10, the company is rolling out disease-specific content on the Calm app and online. The resources include calming meditation and soundscape sessions, which could help those with an advanced cancer diagnosis, for example, "ease moments of distress" and "move to a more empowered state," according to the oncology-specific mindfulness tools page from Calm, Gilead and Kite Oncology. Caregivers or people otherwise impacted by the disease are also encouraged to use the free tools. 

The new partnership falls under Gilead’s “commitment to the whole person,” the company’s V.P. of U.S. public affairs Darius Kuras told Fierce in an interview. The drugmaker’s plethora of medicines for the conditions the program focuses on “only go so far” to help on a whole-person level, especially when it comes to mental health. 

“The idea of marrying the science and the medicine with the support around stress, anxiety, fatigue, particularly for those conditions that we work in—in HIV, in oncology, liver disease—it really made a lot of sense,” Kuras explained. 

Related

Insulet, Calm join forces for diabetes care offerings with ‘Mind in Range’ wellness tools

To develop the content, Gilead worked with patient and patient groups directly to see what kind of support they might need that goes “beyond the medicine,” he said. By leveraging Calm’s global reach of millions of users to deploy helpful mental health resources, visibility around the “quieter issue” can be brought to the forefront, Kuras explained.  

The Calm partnership will extend for two years and could continue to expand as Gilead hones in on its commitment to holistic health. At Gilead, providing resources that “see beyond the physical health” has always been “top of mind,” the V.P. notes. 

Calm made its foray into the biopharma world earlier this year through a collaboration with medtech company Insulet, rolling out a suite of mindfulness tools tailored to the diabetes community. The relaxation app launched in 2012 and has since evolved from a “meditation app into a mental health app,” Chris Mosunic, Ph.D., who serves as chief clinical officer at Calm’s clinical healthcare offshoot Calm Health, explained in an interview earlier this summer. 

In 2023, Calm began tinkering with disease-specific community programming with a Mayo Clinic partnership, offering digital mental health programs to guide cancer patients through anxiety and depression care. Mosunic cited the Insulet collab as a first in the pharma world, however, as an example of a company “leaning into that mental health aspects in a really big way,” he said. “That’s really going to close the gap.”
